title: Consistent hashing

definition.text: A hashing technique that lets a hash table be resized while remapping only about n/m keys on average, where n is the number of keys and m the number of slots.

facts.text: In an ordinary hash table the key-to-slot mapping is a modulo operation, so changing the number of slots (servers) remaps nearly all keys, and reassigning everything is expensive.
Consistent hashing hashes both the keys and the servers onto a circle, and assigns each key to the next server found clockwise from it.
When a server fails or is added, only the keys next to it on the circle move; adding the nth server relocates only a 1/n fraction of the keys.
It spreads cache keys evenly across shards even if some fail; DynamoDB and Cassandra use it to minimize data movement during rebalancing, and CDNs use it to spread content over edge servers.
To stay available and durable, consistent hashing replicates each data item on N nodes, where N is the replication factor; in eventually consistent systems the copies are made asynchronously.

In theory it spreads load evenly, but in practice load is often uneven and one server can become a hotspot; it also adds complexity, risks cascading failures, and makes key management costly when nodes transiently fail.
Karger et al. introduced consistent hashing as the basis of caching protocols that relieve hot spots on very large networks such as the Internet, where delays caused by hot spots can be severe.
A consistent hash function changes minimally as its range changes, so the caching protocols need no current, or even consistent, view of the whole network and scale gracefully as it grows.

notes: From the 1997 paper (abstract only); folds into the Consistent hashing entry from part01 and part02.

title: Rendezvous hashing
article: Consistent hashing#Comparison with rendezvous hashing and other alternatives

definition.text: A simpler and more general technique than consistent hashing, designed in 1996, that lets distributed parties agree on k options out of n using the highest random weight (HRW) algorithm.

facts.text: Rendezvous hashing was designed in 1996 and permits fully distributed agreement on a set of k options out of a possible set of n options.
It reaches the goals of consistent hashing through the very different highest random weight (HRW) algorithm.
Consistent hashing can be shown to be a special case of rendezvous hashing.
Because of its simplicity and generality, rendezvous hashing is now used in place of consistent hashing in many applications.

notes: No Wikipedia page for Rendezvous hashing was crawled; article anchors the comparison section of Consistent hashing.

definition.text: A partition is a division of a logical database or its constituent elements into distinct, independent parts.

facts.text: Database partitioning means deliberately breaking a large database into smaller ones for scalability, which is distinct from a network partition, a type of network fault between nodes.
In a partitioned database each piece of data (record, row or document) belongs to exactly one partition, so each partition is effectively a small database of its own.
Partitioning is normally done for manageability, performance, availability or load balancing, spreading datasets across multiple disks and query loads across multiple processors.

A query that touches a single partition runs independently on that partition's node, so query throughput scales linearly with added nodes; more complex queries can be parallelized across nodes, with extra challenges.
Partitioning is commonly combined with replication: each record belongs to one partition but exists on several nodes, and a node can lead some partitions while following others.
Systems name partitions differently: shard in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and SolrCloud, region in HBase, tablet in Bigtable, vnode in Cassandra and Riak, vBucket in Couchbase.

definition.text: Skew is uneven distribution of data or load across partitions, and a partition that receives excessive load is called a hot spot.

facts.text: Partitioning aims to spread data and query load evenly; with ideal distribution capacity scales linearly, so ten nodes process ten times the data and throughput of one node, while skew reduces that efficiency.
Hot spots can be countered by assigning records to nodes at random (at the cost of harder retrieval), by key-range partitioning with optimized boundaries, or by hash-based partitioning for even load.
With timestamp keys in a sensor network, writes concentrate in the current time period's partition; prefixing the timestamp with the sensor identifier in a compound key spreads that load.

title: Partitioning criteria

definition.text: The rules a database uses to assign each row to a partition from its partitioning key: range, list, composite, round-robin or hash.

facts.text: Relational database systems take a partitioning key and assign a partition by a criterion: range, list, composite, round-robin or hash partitioning.
List partitioning gives each partition a list of values; a row whose key is in the list goes there, as when Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Denmark form a partition for the Nordic countries.
Composite partitioning combines schemes, for example applying range partitioning first and then hash partitioning; consistent hashing can be seen as a composite of hash and list partitioning.

Round-robin partitioning sends the ith tuple in insertion order to partition (i mod n), giving uniform distribution and parallel sequential access, but reaching tuples by a predicate means accessing the entire relation.

A sharding key is a column of the table, and the sharding algorithm uses it to decide which shard stores each row; choosing the right key and algorithm is crucial for even distribution and performance.
Directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table (directory) that maps sharding keys to shard locations, and routes data by consulting it.

Consistent hashing extends hash-based sharding to move less data when shards change; virtual bucket sharding maps data to virtual buckets and buckets to physical shards, easing rebalancing without much data movement.
When shards follow a real-world segmentation, such as European versus American customers, the right shard can be inferred easily and only that shard queried.

notes: Wikipedia's partitioning criteria and ByteByteGo's and Singh's sharding algorithms are the same concept; folded into one entry.

definition.text: Range partitioning assigns continuous ranges of the partitioning key to partitions, like the volumes of an encyclopedia.

facts.text: Because the range boundaries are known, a request can be routed straight to the partition that holds its key.
Boundaries can be set manually or automatically so that the data is balanced across partitions.
Range partitioning makes range scans efficient, but certain access patterns, such as writing time-ordered keys, create hot spots.
A typical example is a partition for all rows whose zipcode column has a value between 70000 and 79999.
Ranges must be contiguous but not overlapping; each has a non-inclusive lower and upper bound, and key values at or above a range's upper bound go to the next partition.

Range-based sharding works on ordered columns such as integers, longs or timestamps, for example customers by alphabetical order of last name, transactions by date range, or user IDs 1 to 1000 in shard 1.

definition.text: Hash partitioning applies a hash function to the partitioning key, turning skewed data into a uniform distribution so that load spreads evenly across partitions.

facts.text: It effectively prevents hot spots, but it sacrifices range query efficiency because adjacent keys scatter across partitions.
Common implementations use MD5, as Cassandra and MongoDB do.
Cassandra combines both approaches with compound primary keys: the first component is hashed to pick the partition, while the remaining components keep sort order within the partition.
A shard key such as a customer ID or transaction ID is hashed, which tends to spread data more evenly than range-based sharding, but a proper hash function is needed to avoid collisions.
A simple form is shard_id = hash(user_id) % num_shards, but dynamically adding or removing database servers then becomes expensive, which is the problem consistent hashing solves.

title: Horizontal partitioning

definition.text: Horizontal partitioning puts different rows of a table into different tables.

facts.text: For example, customers with ZIP codes below 50000 go in CustomersEast and those at 50000 or above in CustomersWest; a view with a union over both tables gives the complete picture of all customers.
Holding fewer rows in each table reduces index size, which generally improves search performance.
It pays off when there is an obvious, robust and implicit way to tell which partition holds a row without searching the index, as a ZIP code does.

Many guides use horizontal partitioning and sharding as synonyms: a table is divided into smaller tables, each a separate data store with the same columns but fewer rows, so more machines can share the load.

notes: Wikipedia separates horizontal partitioning (usually one schema instance and server) from sharding (several instances); ByteByteGo and Singh treat the two as one thing.

definition.text: Vertical partitioning creates tables with fewer columns and stores the remaining columns in additional tables, so rows are split by their columns.

facts.text: It goes beyond normalization by splitting columns even when the table is already normalized; it is also called row splitting.
Infrequently used or very wide columns that take up much memory can be moved to a different machine.
A common form splits static data from dynamic data, since the static part is faster to access; a view across the two tables restores the original table at a performance penalty.
A columnar database can be regarded as a database vertically partitioned until each column is stored in its own table.

definition.text: A database shard is a horizontal partition of the data in a database or search engine, and each shard may be held on a separate database server instance.

facts.text: Each shard is the single source for its subset of data, and placing shards on separate hardware spreads a database across many machines, which can significantly improve performance.

Splitting tables over servers reduces the rows per table and the index size, which generally improves search, and the search load spreads over multiple servers rather than only over several indexes on one server.
Plain horizontal partitioning stays within one schema instance and server, while sharding partitions the table the same way across potentially multiple instances of the schema.
Sharding distributes large partitionable tables across servers while smaller tables are replicated in full on each server, and a mechanism is needed to keep the replicated tables synchronized.
Sharding relates to shared-nothing architecture, since each shard can sit in its own schema instance, server, data center or region, and it aims to minimize cross-shard access.
Every shard has the same schema and columns but holds a unique, independent subset of the data, and all shards together contain all of the data.
Sharding logic can live in the application, in a middleware layer between application and database, or in the database system itself.

Shards give logical independence, since each can be managed on its own for availability, and sensitive and non-sensitive data can be kept in different partitions for better manageability and security.

definition.text: Sharding adds complexity to the database infrastructure and application code, which brings several costs: harder queries, more software that can fail, and more demanding failover, backup and schema management.

facts.text: Developers may need to write more complex SQL queries to handle the sharding logic.
The software that partitions, balances, coordinates and maintains data integrity can itself fail or introduce errors.
Corruption or failure of one shard can affect the integrity of the entire dataset, and fail-over servers must maintain copies of all shards.
Backups of the individual shards must be coordinated with each other, and adding indexes, modifying columns or altering the schema all become harder.

Joins that span several shards are often not feasible or not efficient, because the data must be retrieved from multiple servers; transactions across shards may need distributed transaction management.
When distribution is uneven or one shard is heavily loaded, shards must be rebalanced, and changing the sharding scheme after the database is sharded is complex and time-consuming.
The ORDER BY operation gets more complicated: data is usually fetched from different shards and sorted in the application's code.
Uneven distribution can leave some shards holding more data than others, which is also called a hotspot.

title: Virtual nodes

definition.text: A virtual node (vnode) is an existing physical node mapped multiple times across the hash ring, so that its share of the key space is made of several small ranges.

facts.text: Instead of one position, a physical node is given several smaller ranges of the hash range; the number of duplicate labels a server gets is its weight.

Without them a failed server's keys all move to the next server clockwise, potentially doubling its load; with several positions per server, its keys are reassigned to different servers, spreading them more evenly.
Virtual nodes spread load more evenly across physical nodes, speed up rebalancing after nodes are added or removed, and lower the probability of hotspots.
Multiple labels are needed because servers are not uniformly distributed around the circle, which causes skew among nodes.

notes: Wikipedia names this under variance reduction; Singh and Cassandra and Riak call it a vnode (sent 6468f06ccfdd).

definition.text: Sharding is worth using when one machine cannot hold the data or serve the requests and other optimizations are not enough, because scaling out is then cheaper than scaling up.

facts.text: Sharding is generally recommended only when other optimization strategies have proven insufficient; sharding a table before it has been optimized locally adds needless complexity.
After a certain point it is cheaper and more feasible to scale horizontally by adding machines than to scale vertically by adding more powerful servers.
Sharding solves a single server holding too much data, serving too many requests, and rising query latency as data grows.

Singh lists reasons to shard: using existing hardware instead of high-end machines, keeping data in distinct geographic regions, scaling quickly by adding shards, lighter load per machine, and more concurrent connections.

title: Database federation

definition.text: Federation, also called functional partitioning, splits up databases by function.

facts.text: A federation makes several distinct physical databases appear as one logical database to end users, tied together by federated schemas that express the commonality of data and specify what the components may share.
It gives a cohesive, unified view of data from multiple sources, which can include databases and other structured and unstructured data.

A federated database is transparent, so users need not know where data is stored; it copes with differing hardware, protocols and data models; and it leaves existing data sources and their interfaces unchanged.
Advantages are flexible data sharing, autonomy among components, unified access to heterogeneous data, and no tight coupling of applications with legacy databases.
Disadvantages are extra hardware and complexity, complex joins of data from two databases, dependence on autonomous data sources, and query performance and scalability limits.

notes: Singh's section opens with functional partitioning (split by function) but its body describes a federated database, one logical view over several possibly heterogeneous databases; both are stated as Singh gives them.
